title: Taking a Gap Year
description: A radio introduction, a family discussion, an interview with a returned traveller and a talk from a university adviser about gap years.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · Radio feature: What is a gap year?
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter introducing a feature about gap years.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Welcome to Student Life. Today we're looking at a question that thousands of young people ask themselves every spring: should I take a year out before university?

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: The idea of a gap year began in Britain, where school leavers would spend twelve months travelling or working before they started their degrees. Today it's popular all over the world, although the way people spend the time has changed a great deal.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: In the past, most gap years were about travel, and many students went to faraway countries to volunteer. Now more young people choose to work at home to save money, because university has become so expensive.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Supporters say that a gap year makes students more mature. Studies suggest that students who take a year out often get better marks in their first year, probably because they are more motivated and know what they want to study.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Critics, however, worry that it's easy to lose the study habit. Some students find it hard to return to the classroom, and a few never go back at all.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: So who is right? Later in the programme we'll hear from a student who is just back from a year abroad, but first, let's listen to one family who couldn't agree.

parts.title: Part 2 · A family discussion
parts.intro: You will hear a father, Mr Brown, talking with his daughter, Emma, about her plans.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: Dad, I've made a decision. I'd like to defer my place at university and take a gap year.

script.speaker: Dad
script.text: Oh. Well, that's a surprise. I thought you were looking forward to starting in September.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: I am, in a way. But honestly, I'm tired. I've worked non-stop for two years, and I don't even know if I've chosen the right course.

script.speaker: Dad
script.text: That's exactly what worries me. If you have doubts, why not start and change course later? Plenty of students do.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: And waste a year of fees if it goes wrong? That seems much riskier to me.

script.speaker: Dad
script.text: Hmm, I hadn't thought of it that way. What would you actually do for twelve months? I'm not paying for a long holiday.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: I wouldn't expect you to. My plan is to work in a hotel for six months to save money. Then I'd spend the rest of the year volunteering at a school in Vietnam, which is where Grandma grew up.

script.speaker: Dad
script.text: That does sound more serious than I imagined. And you'd improve your Vietnamese, which would please your grandmother.

script.speaker: Emma
script.text: Exactly. So you're not against it?

script.speaker: Dad
script.text: I'm not against it, but I'd like you to write the plan down, with the dates and the costs. If it holds together on paper, I'll support you.

parts.title: Part 3 · Interview with a returned traveller
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Linh, interviewing a student, Jack, who has just returned from a gap year.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Jack, you've just come back from a year in South America. How would you describe it?

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: Honestly, it was the best and the hardest year of my life. I went with a friend, but after two months we argued and went separate ways, which was frightening at first.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: That sounds stressful. What did you do on your own?

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: I joined a farm project in the mountains, picking coffee. I'd never worked with my hands before, and the first week my back ached terribly. But I learned Spanish quickly because nobody there spoke English.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Did you ever think about coming home early?

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: Once, in about the fourth month. I got ill, and I felt very far from my family. But a local family looked after me, and that experience is what I remember best, much more than any famous sights I saw.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Many people say a gap year is just an expensive holiday. What do you say to that?

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: I'd say it depends on you. If you only visit tourist places and take photographs, then yes. But if you take risks, work and meet people, it changes you. I'm more patient now, and I'm certainly less shy.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: And are you ready to study again?

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: More than I expected. I start in three weeks, and I'm looking forward to sitting in a library again. I never thought I'd say that.

parts.title: Part 4 · Advice from a university adviser
parts.intro: You will hear a university adviser, Mr Nam Tran, giving advice to students at a school.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Good afternoon, everyone. I've spoken to hundreds of students about gap years, so let me give you some practical advice, whichever way you decide.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: First, check the rules of your university. Many universities allow you to keep your place for a year, but you usually have to ask before a certain date, and some courses, such as medicine, are stricter than others.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Second, set a goal. Students who say, I'll see what happens, often end up doing nothing. You don't need an exciting project, but you should be able to explain in one sentence why you are taking the time.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Third, think about money. A gap year doesn't have to be expensive. Some of the most useful experiences, such as working in a local business, actually pay you. Others, like organised volunteering trips abroad, can cost thousands, and I'd be careful with companies that charge very high fees.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Fourth, keep a record. Write down what you learn and the skills you gain. When you apply for jobs later, employers will be much more interested in a specific example than in a general statement that you travelled.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Finally, don't see a gap year as an escape from a decision. It's not for everyone, and there's no shame in going straight to university. The best choice is the one that you have thought about carefully.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: If you'd like to talk it through, my office is open on Wednesday mornings, and no appointment is needed.
